And I wasn't up back with your band until I heard a little bit of that as all. But Ralph told me more about it. Just what do you do? Do you follow the melody and start in your mind? Yeah, in your mind. Play a regular chorus or something?
Yeah, that's right. Just follow that melody. And most of the time I'd be counting to myself, you know.
You were playing snare drum, I guess, were you at that time? No, bass drum.
Bass drum.
Bass drum. I can't even remember.

Baptiste was playing the bass drum. Oh, we'd only do it because I have never tried it on snare drum with nobody else. I play snare on some of the parades, but I have never tried that with anyone else.
You always play the bass drum on those solo.
Yeah. Yeah. That's about the only fellow I imagine that I could do it with, with that. I have never tried it with nobody else.
I wish I could hear some more of that this year. I hope you all get out again. Keep playing much more. I hope we get out again.
You'll hear it. I hope you all get out again.
I hope you all get out again.
In fact, he's the only one I like to play bass drum on the street with. He's a fine drummer, fine, fine drummer.
Oh, that Sam Morgan band, Back to Them. What did they play? Were they playing regular parades or funnels?
Yeah, regular parades and funnels they played them, yeah. Because I have second line behind them on many occasions.
How many brass bands were there when you were second line?
Well, it was Sam Morgan band during that time, the Tuxedo Brass Band and the Olympia Brass Band.
Those were the main ones that you thought? Yeah.

Now, the Olympia, I remember Willie Humphrey was playing back in that band and Bill Maffrey was playing snare drum. And Charlie Love, he was in that band too. Now, I'm not sure now, I really, I believe O'Man Petit was in that band too at the time.
The drum roll band?
Yeah, I believe he was in that band.
The Tuxedo, you remember pretty well those guys?

Oh yeah, I remember Eddie Jackson, I remember Bikku, I remember uh, Poppin, Albert Snighed, what else? Some of the guys I just came, I think called them. And uh, the bass drum player, uh, Trepanion, what you call him in this? Trepanion.
He usually just played bass drum in parades or snare, or whatever? Trepanion?
Uh huh. Well, he used to play orchestra too, they tell me, but I have never heard of him in orchestra, but I know of him playing bass drum, he was a fine bass drum player too, very funny.
It must have been about 1932 you started, I got messed up on my audition back then.
I just don't remember this when you started, I got depressed.
I guess it was after the depression hit.
Well it was, if it was, it wasn't too far, too long.
The drums were pretty hard.
Were you ever in that WPA band, that big band? No, no, no, I never did get a chance of that.
Did you go over all the other old time drummers like Henry Zeno? That's too far back. Is that too far back? No, I don't know him. That old man Cottrell, did you hear him?

Well I heard of him and in fact I saw him one time on the street. And Red Allen played bass drum that particular day, played a few of them. I remember singing, waste time of it, because I asked who the old man was and they told me who he was.

You know something I've often wondered is, who were the drummers that could really swing but play very soft? Some bands get down real low and the drummers are really swinging, but not loud. I think Joseph Frasier was the one. I didn't even hear him. But I think that's probably the way he used to do it. You can tell the way he's doing it now. It can really come down. Some drummers it's... I never did hear him, but I think he got that ability.
I think Joe René was a soft drummer. Yeah, yeah. Joe René. I think he was a soft drummer.
Yeah, well some guys can play so well and have a lot of feeling and still they don't have to play fast or loud.
Well Joe René was one of the type that could do. I see.
We talked about Chani before, and Red Happy and Faiso. Some of the other drummers you've heard.
Well I was two of the rough type of drummers, they were rough, man.
What about Alfred Williams back then, what did he play?
Alfred was a nice drummer too, he was, I would say in between, you know, maybe soft and, you know, mild. And Rudolph was a soft drummer too. Yeah.
With Rudolph, Big Rudolph.
Yeah, he was a soft drummer too.
What does rough mean when you're talking about a drummer?

What does rough drummers do? Well I mean it's guys that could blast so loud and get so much out of those bass drums with those awkward foot pedals that they had, see how they could do it. In fact I never had a chance to play on none of them, to use none of them, because I wasn't playing the boat drums. In fact it just was going out during that time. I would love to get one of them myself and see how it would work.
I'd like to hear you play on the tambourine on your drum. That would be interesting to hear that.

Well they used that just like a, looked like a tum tum too, you know, just hit licks on it. It's not. Hold it up in one hand or have it down? No, no, they had it, some kind of way they had it clamped on the side of the bass.
That might be a good novelty now. Yeah.
I was thinking of it myself, but getting the one. I tried.
Those heads are pretty thin, any danger of breaking the head if you hit on it with the stick flex?
Well I couldn't say because I never played none of them. I don't know just how hard the guys was hitting them. I used to see them hit them, but I don't know how hard they were hitting them.
They're not too easy to break, Bill. Not too easy, huh?
Mm-hmm. Hit on the rim and all too and make a lot of the jingle noise. Is there anything you can tell us about the drum sets and the way of when they began using the hi-hat or the sock cymbals?

Well the only thing I can say about that, Bill, is I had a chance to use one of the sock cymbals that they used during those days. It was a low-low cymbal. I said about this high up, what you would say, about a foot high. And the guys used to use that, but they never had a chance to use it. The two of those didn't work the stick on it at all? No, no, no, they didn't work the stick on it at all.
Frog, when you started, did you have a sock cymbal too in your outfit?
Yeah, but it was high.
It was up high.

Let me ask Frog about something. Did you get anything about his brother, Ferdinand? Not so much. Who is your brother Ferdinand? I wanted to know more about him. You mentioned him once. Well, I can tell you. I know he made this record with Papa, my Joan of Fiend. He made it up the On Canal Street at the Decker deal. Well, he can tell you more about it.
We have his address, we'll try to talk to him.

Yeah, and he's saying... Well, when you do, let me make an appointment with him, you know. Yeah, well that would be a good one. So you'll be sure to get him, you know. Yeah, I do that. And did you ask him anything about the El Morocco?
The club up here, you know? Mm-hmm.

Well, Bourbon Street? Yeah. I worked there with George. He played with all of you. Oh, wow. Only a few nights. What style were you playing before you went with George? Commercial music, anything come up. Anything? Reading? I've done everything in music but play a parade or funeral. I wasn't. I wasn't ill. Mm-hmm. Well, definitely reading, that's for sure. I see. Yeah. Did you play any of the old New Orleans style music before you got with George? We used to do it. With Freddie Band before we got on the street. Oh, yeah, I see. But not as many tunes but we used to do it now. Mm-hmm. Before this music got back, you know? Mm-hmm. I see. Yeah, I have just a couple of things I wanted to ask him about when I was at home. Uh, back to Chester. I did think of one thing I didn't ask you. Who were some of your favorite clarinet players, I'd say, when you were quite young going around?
Well, just like I've always told you, I wasn't too much interested in other guys in the band. All I was interested in was the drumming. Drumming was the only thing I was interested in.
You never paid much attention to trombone or clarinet?
No, no, never paid much attention. A trumpet at all?
No.

A trumpet maybe, I might have paid. You know, I still like trumpet, the way guys blow trumpet. I remember a time back, I remember Punch when he was playing, Kid Rene, Chris Kelly. Nah, I heard Guy Kelly a couple of times. I was like, yeah, yeah, yeah. And, uh, I always liked Rene's style of playing. Loved his style of playing. Down the late days, like I told you, came up with this fella, Kiefer. I went wild about his style of playing.
It's funny, I don't know a thing about him. Bill, did you ever hear good guy? No.
You know who he played? I don't think so. He's from Algiers, boy. He's from Ovin' Algiers.
You know him at all? No, I heard of him. I believe Fred introduced me to him. But he did. Flying trumpet man.
Now, if you could ask him more about the other drummers, I don't know who you've talked about, but what about the Matthew boys, how many of those did you hear?
Bill Matthews? Well, I heard Bill a couple of times play drum on the street.
He played last year, I think he played Isidore Barbera. Paul's father, you know when he died, he played this funeral on drums, didn't he?
I believe so, I'm not sure. Yeah, pretty sure.
I think I might some mind said he played drums.
He was down with Eureka at the Armistice Day one time at Chalmette.
I was wondering, you know, also about Ramis and Bebe.

Well, I played bass drum with Ramis. Ramis played snare drum and I played bass drum with them already. But I never played, I wasn't playing when Bill was playing drums, snare drum when he was playing drums. I wasn't playing.
Oh, that's something I wanted to ask you while we're on that subject, of street drums. When you started out, who played the cymbal, the snare drum or the bass drum? Oh, the bass drum.
The cymbal was always on the bass drum.
I see. And how big a cymbal was it?
Well, just about the same sound we were using now.
Same thing now, that didn't change? No, it hasn't changed.
And what did he hit it with? Well a lot of times we made a, just taking a coat hanger off, a piece of white and made a rim.
Same thing. What about Henry Martin? Do you remember? Oh yeah, I remember him. He was a fine bass drum player. Was he mostly in parades or dance bands? Where did you hear him?
I never know of him playing in the orchestra in a band, I mean all I know of him playing bass drum rather than snare on him.
Yeah. Which band did he work with when you heard him, do you remember?
No, just Olympia Brass Band, I think it was.
Did you ever hear Manu Perez? Oh yeah.
Second line behind him many times.
What band was he with?
Well, Henry was playing with his band. Manu was with his band too. Now what was the name of that band, I don't remember.
Did Black Benny play with dance bands or did you tell him he did or didn't?
I don't know. They said he did. He used to play both of the drums but I never saw him. And you saw him with Sam Morgan and who else?
Anybody else?
Well that's about the only band I ever saw him.
There's another fellow who played drums, I never, I met him in Chicago, a friend of Louis Armstrong's, Little Joe Lindsey. Well I know of him.
Did you ever hear him on drums? I never did hear him. No, I never hear him either. I know of him but I know too much about him.
I think he worked at the Absinthe House was it?
Yeah, that's where I met him. I was introduced to him through Kid Howard. Kid Howard's the one introduced me to him.
I think Kid Ory once had him and his band in place of Henry Martin had been Ory's drummer but he seemed to like Joe Lindsey too I believe if I remember.
Well when Kid Ory was down here I don't remember Kid Ory.
No but I thought maybe Henry, I mean Joe Lindsey might have played quite a while later. You never heard him then in your time?
No, I never heard him.
What about Tom Coleman? I never did get, you tell me about him.
Thomas Coleman. He's played string bass and bass tuba. He was a fine tuba player too.
Who did he play with?
The same for Willie Parker's band. He used to play at two of them Willie Parker's band. Now he was playing string bass with Sam Morgan's band also. Thomas Coleman. Thomas Coleman.
Now who else did he play string bass with?
Well I saw him go up.
Now where was he from? You say some kind of alligator.
Yeah, he's a distant cousin or something. He's from now and the Cut Ory too. I'm already sure that's the way he's from.
It's interesting, there's a lot of musicians from down in that neighborhood.
Yeah, the drum one player, what's his name, Luchi? Luchi? Yeah, he's from now and that way.
Well Saeed's not from now and that way.
I don't know if Saeed's from now and that way. Saeed? No, I don't know if he's from now and that way.
I don't know if he's from now and that way. Well I mean Dave, all Dave, a relation, they're from now and that way. Yeah.
I know Luchi from now and that way. I know Luchi from now and that way.
Just some of the real old timers like Tom Albert came from now.
Well I think Tom is from now and that way too.

Maybe Eddie Vincent, the real old time trombonist, that was before your time too, was it Frog? I guess he played with Keppard and people like that. I guess so, Bill, I don't know. Yeah, he left here long before you were born.
Now Tom Albert was another man, one of the old men's in the Eureka band, one of the Eureka bands we started up to. Yeah, he was.
A lot of guys from Deerrange and Magnolia.

I'm about to run out of questions, Bill. Yeah, I can't think of many more. Did you cover all the different bands you played with? Yes. Yeah, we covered all that. We did. All about your family? Were there any other members of your family that played?
No, outside of me, my father and my son.
Oh, say back during the 30's after you got with Kid Howard, did you play many spots with other bands?

No, mostly I was with Kid Howard. Well, where did you play with Kid Howard? I played rhythm club, I played the signing, signings club, I played picnics, weddings and different things, so on and so forth. So down to Grand Island. Never played theater? No, I never played theater in my life.

Frog and I were talking about some of the things that make New Orleans music different than other things. Like he mentioned the melody and the fact that they get together, play together and a few other things as well. Another thing, as he said, his father told him about to be able to play any type of music. Is there anything, remarks you'd have about the particular kind of drumming that you've noticed? Any other drummers away from here that they're different than the fellows here, their beat or anything, if you could explain, have you noticed any difference in the New Orleans style of drumming you might say, compared to say the way they do up north or other places?

Well no, I have never heard any of the guys playing all this music away from here. The only time I was away from here, Bill, when I was with Artie Crossley's band, I went to Los Angeles and played out there. Oh yeah. And in fact, we were the only band, they had the bandage to play there on Sundays, but I had never went down to here. So I couldn't say anything about the guys playing drums.

Have you ever had any experience of other drummers from outside of town coming in here and trying to play with some of your bands and noticed that they played differently or? No. Anything much about, different style or anything? No, I haven't. Is there anything that you can make any remarks about the New Orleans music? Things that you try to do with your drumming? What do you think the drums are your main job in the band? Like is it just keeping time or anything else that you could say is your job in the band? What would you...

No, Bill, the only thing I could say about that when I'm playing is the feelings I get. Something that's come to me, I just try to make it. If I fail at it, I just won't forget about it and try it another time. In the old...
Did they have many drum solos that you can remember?

All these drum solos, I remember the guys after the last chorus, just before they're going out, the guy might come back with a full bar. The guys start back again like we do today. Yeah, did you ever have any name for that? All those solos are like these guys doing now. I don't remember that. I don't remember that at all.
Did you have any name for that little ending you put on there? Any special thing you called it or anything?

No, I used to remember the guys saying, I used to go to St. Alex and Adam, after finishing the number, people would be applauding for it to play the tune over again. God said, watch them, let's fool. And they start right back on it. This drum would start off and then they start playing that number again.
I remember Baby Dodge used to call it a drum tag. He'd call it a tag that they put on.
That's the only thing I used to remember the guys saying, let's fool them. That song is starting right back over again.
I've heard people call it a turnaround. That's what Paul Crawford called it. It's really a tag.
It's really a tag.

You've heard that word? Yeah, it is. It's a tag. A tag, yeah. I didn't know if it was common that everybody called it that. Well, it's a tag and it's a turnaround. So it's a sound. Damn, Dave. Well, one other thing I was going to ask about, the thing that I noticed when I came down here from the north originally to hear the bands at the dances is that quite often they play the whole piece over. I mean, people applaud me, so they start and play the whole piece over at the encore. Did they do that in the old days? That's right. Do you remember when you were young?
That's right. That's the way they did it.
Is it fairly common that they do that almost every set? Would they repeat two or three numbers or how often would they do that?

Well, I wouldn't say every set. I mean, maybe one or two numbers and then they'll do it, you know. I think it's according to the way the fathers was feeling if they had liked that number themselves, that particular number, when they'd do it over. But if something that didn't, you know, really, it's just like you, if you like something, a number you like, and it was time for you to go out on that number, you go out and look like you're just beginning to get that feeling that you want to play more of it. See, you know, and all the guys, I think, during that time, that's the way they felt about us. It's one thing I say this much, though, about the young musicians. When they work, they really play for the people. Yeah, that's right. Yeah. Because I have worked at other places, and it's no different. I work a certain place in Chicago. I mean, you don't get no requests. You know, actually, I mean, that don't mean nothing. Yeah.

You know, that Fulham business reminds me. When I used to go here, Joe Avery and Wilbert Tillman up at Towers, Big Garden up by Adam and Buck, I don't know if he ever said it. But they'd play a number, and they'd come to the end, and they'd stop. Now, I don't know how many, whether they'd just stop for a bar or two. And then all of a sudden, they'd start up again, and it was a way of Fulham,
but nobody would do anything.
What do you call that?
Not when they'd stop like that, with the drummers.
Nobody was. Just complete silence.
Did you ever hear that, Bill? I've heard some breaks, though. I don't know whether it's intentional. What do you say that one?
No, Bache does it. Bache does that on Shake It and Break It. That record, I don't know if you remember it. But the band will stop.
Oh, you mean that's a break.

No, no. Nobody's. You mean it's a break? No, not a break. But they come to the end of the chorus, and then stop, and everybody thinks the tune is over, and then they start up again after a certain number of beats. I forget.
Was that a taxi dance for you? Somebody was working on it?
No, it wasn't a taxi dance.

Well, what he's talking about, that's just trying to... The thing I was saying about this guy... It's like Putin. Like a tag. When they come to that, and everybody stop, man. And all of a sudden, the drum pick up. Then they start right on back with that number again. I have seen them do that a lot of times, occasionally.
Another thing I noticed when I first heard New Orleans bands is that you don't notice that in other cities and up north is the stomping off business.
Oh, they always did that down in the old time.
Knock off to go out. Yeah, I remember.
Yeah. And before they got there, you give it that.
Now, where should that, when you knock off, or whatever you call it, where should that be? Right before the last course, or as you start the last course?
Where's the correct place? I mean, knocking off to go out? Yeah, to go out. Well, I mean, everybody having fun. If the leader don't knock off, I could continue playing. Yeah.
I mean, when should he give you that signal? Right before the last course?
Right before the last course. Right before you start. Oh, now, probably the tune might run. The way the tune might run might be the last eight.
Could be then. Sometimes he stops.
The majority of the time at the last course.
Yeah, the whole chorus.
I think we're the honest one using that now. We do it sometimes.

But I wonder if the leader gave the stomp in the middle of the chorus there. Well, it'll go out. And that's the end. That's the end. That's the end. That's the end. That's the end. That's the end. That's the end. Yeah, when he do that. That's the end. Right there. You wouldn't play another one after that if you were about halfway through and he stopped it. And you finish up then. That's right. Because I thought it might be a signal then to go another whole course. I didn't know if they had any special signal.
It's a pretty good thing for cats just getting back to what we were talking about. You know, you call people up on the phone and you just get together. So you've got to ask some kind of rude things.
They don't know those things other parts of the country. I've ever heard.
We use a whole lot of old time things out there. Do this.
Oh, yeah. Hold it.
Another one.
Hold the hand.
Put this on him. That's four bar. Four bar break.
Four fingers means a four bar break.
Four bar tag for him. Oh, yeah. Alright, that's football tag for him. And we'll do that. That's football tag for him and we're going to play the last eight.

I see. One thing I wondered about waltzes here too. In olden times when you played a waltz Chester and you play it in waltz time, what would happen then if the people applauded after it? Would you go play it in 4-4 or 3-4?
I would play it right back the same way. The same way? Yeah. And then now probably if they still applauded, then you go back in that 3-4, that 4-4.
Now I notice they stop it and then wait a second or a while and then they'll play it in 4-4.
Sometimes they'll stop the 3-4 right in the middle and go into the 4-4.
You hear it both ways. Sometimes they stop in between. That's about the end of the tape.
Yeah, about another half a minute. Unless there's some other remark you all have. Any other idea you have on the style of the music, Chester? Especially we talked it over at Frogger, did you?
All right, I'll be right now, Bill. I just couldn't think of anything. Unless some question you asked me probably might come to me.

Sort of run out of questions. I think I quit that everything. No, no, it covered your life. What the tells me to have your life down, I'm sure. Very nice ideas on the music, too, which we're always interested in hearing about.
Yeah, and it helps us place things in time. Time to talk to the younger guys. Let me see when they... ... ... ...
